Newborn Care

When your baby does not want a pacifier

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A pacifier can seem like the missing answer when you need to settle a baby or take a moment to yourself. Then your baby spits it out, turns away or looks offended by the offer. Some babies enjoy sucking a pacifier, some accept it only occasionally, and some never want one. You can explore the option without turning acceptance into a task your baby has to complete.

First check what your baby needs

A pacifier offers sucking without milk. That can be comforting after feeding needs are met, but it cannot answer hunger. Before offering one, consider whether your baby needs a feed, a diaper change, a quieter space, a change in temperature or contact with you.

Crying is information, even when the reason is hard to work out. Do not use a pacifier to stretch the time between feeds or suppress hunger cues because a schedule says it is too early. A baby who repeatedly refuses milk or seems unwell needs attention to that problem, not more practice with a pacifier.

When is a reasonable time to introduce one?

For a directly breastfed baby, wait until breastfeeding is established before routine pacifier use. Effective feeding, comfortable attachment, enough milk and appropriate weight gain matter more than a particular birthday. This is often several weeks after birth, but the timing differs between families.

If you are not directly breastfeeding, a pacifier can be offered earlier if you wish. A premature baby or a baby with a feeding difficulty may have a specific care plan, so ask their team. No calendar date can guarantee that introducing a pacifier will prevent every feeding problem or a problem described as “nipple confusion.”

1. Give a new object time: but respect a no

A pacifier is an unfamiliar object with its own shape, feel and movement. Spitting it out on the first attempt does not tell you whether the baby will ever enjoy it. If they are comfortable, you can leave the possibility open and offer it on another occasion.

Patience means allowing time, not repeating the offer until the baby gives in. Turning away, closing the mouth, gagging or becoming more upset are reasons to stop. You do not need a target number of attempts or weeks of persistence. A later offer is optional, and so is deciding you have tried enough.

2. Choose a calm first introduction

A baby who is already crying intensely may not be ready to explore something new. Attend to the immediate need and help them settle first. A relaxed, awake moment can make it easier to notice whether they are interested in the pacifier or simply want to look around.

Offer it gently without pushing it into a closed or resisting mouth. Watch what happens instead of assuming silence is the only successful result. If the baby loses interest, put it away. You can learn something about their preference even when they never begin to suck.

3. Offer after feeding needs are met

When a baby still wants milk, a pacifier is a disappointing substitute. If they seem satisfied after a feed but continue to seek sucking for comfort, that may be a reasonable time to offer one. “After a feed” is an opportunity, not a requirement to introduce a pacifier after every meal.

A recent feed does not prove that a baby cannot be hungry again. Continue to notice cues and the wider feeding pattern. If you are unsure about intake, uncomfortable feeding or weight gain, seek feeding support rather than using the pacifier to test whether the baby really needed more milk.

4. Skip milk coatings and sweeteners

Dipping a pacifier in breast milk or formula is sometimes suggested to make it more appealing. A coating is not needed to teach a baby what the object is for. Offer a clean, uncoated pacifier; NICHD’s safe-sleep guidance advises against coating it with anything.

Never add honey to an infant’s pacifier. Honey can cause infant botulism and should not be given before twelve months. Sugar, syrup and other sweet coatings are not suitable persuasion tools either. Feed milk as part of feeding, and keep an optional comfort object separate from an effort to disguise its taste.

5. Avoid a surprise swap during breastfeeding

Quickly substituting a pacifier for the breast before the baby notices may sound convenient, but it does not tell you that feeding is complete or that the baby wants the substitute. Finish responding to the feeding need first, then make a separate, gentle offer if appropriate.

Touching the cheek can prompt a young baby to turn and search for a feed. That response is not permission to override resistance or a technique you must practise to secure a pacifier. There is no need to trick your baby. Comfort works best when you can notice and respond to what they are showing you.

6. Try another suitable shape if you want to

Pacifiers differ in shape, size and material. A baby may prefer one and reject another. If you choose to try a different model, make sure it is age-appropriate, complies with local safety requirements and is used according to its instructions. A good fit matters more than an impressive marketing description.

You do not need a drawer full of products. Trying endless designs can become expensive and tiring without changing the baby’s preference. Do not improvise with a loose bottle nipple or alter a pacifier to make it smaller or softer. A baby who accepts a bottle is not obliged to enjoy a pacifier.

7. Do not turn sucking into a tugging game

Pulling lightly on a pacifier while it is in the mouth is sometimes promoted as “reverse psychology,” intended to make a baby suck harder to keep it. A reflex response is not evidence that a reluctant baby now wants the object, and you do not need this manoeuvre to provide comfort.

Let the baby suck voluntarily and stop when they release it or resist. Never hold or tape a pacifier in place. Checking a product for loose parts while it is outside the baby’s mouth is a different task from tugging on it during use. Follow the product’s inspection instructions separately.

8. Build a settling routine that works without one

You can feed when needed, hold your baby, speak or sing softly, or gently rock them while you are awake. A quieter setting may help when there has been a lot to see and hear. Try to notice which changes seem welcome; doing more and more at once can make it hard to tell.

Some babies prefer closeness to sucking an object. That is a preference you can work with. If you need a brief break, put the baby on their back in a safe cot or bassinet, step away for a short time and ask a trusted adult for support if available. Never shake a baby, however overwhelmed you feel.

Choose, clean and inspect the product

A one-piece pacifier with a suitable shield reduces the risk of parts separating or the whole object going into the mouth. Follow the age range and local product guidance. Keep packaging and small protective caps out of reach, and do not use a bottle teat as a makeshift pacifier.

Follow the manufacturer’s cleaning and replacement instructions, using clean hands. Inspect the nipple and other parts regularly, and discard an item that is torn, sticky, damaged or deteriorating. If a cleaning method uses heat, allow the item and any trapped water to cool before offering it. Never repair a damaged pacifier for continued use.

Keep the sleep advice in perspective

Offering a pacifier at naps and bedtime is part of AAP and NICHD advice for reducing sudden infant death syndrome risk, once feeding is going well. It is still optional if the baby refuses. If it falls out after the baby is asleep, you do not need to keep putting it back.

A pacifier does not replace the rest of safe sleep: place the baby on their back on a firm, flat, separate infant sleep surface with a fitted sheet and no loose bedding or soft objects. Do not attach a pacifier to clothing, bedding or toys for sleep, and never put a cord around a baby’s neck.

Know when refusal is part of a wider concern

Refusing only a pacifier while feeding well and behaving normally is different from suddenly struggling to suck or refusing feeds too. Seek clinical advice for feeding difficulty, repeated gagging during feeds, poor growth, an unusual persistent cry or a baby who seems unwell. Tell the clinician what changed and when.

Seek urgent medical care for a temperature of 38°C or higher in a baby younger than three months. Breathing difficulty, blue or grey lips, unusual unresponsiveness or a baby who is difficult to wake require emergency help. Do not continue trying a comfort technique while an urgent symptom is present.

You can leave the decision open

If your baby accepts a pacifier later, you can use it thoughtfully without making it the answer to every cry. If they never accept one, there is no pacifier habit to wean, although they may find other ways to soothe themselves. Neither outcome measures your skill as a parent.

For a child who continues using a pacifier, discuss the habit at routine dental care and plan ahead for reducing prolonged use. Duration and frequency matter for developing teeth. For now, the immediate aim is simpler: meet feeding needs, offer comfort and choose safe equipment only when it is welcome.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Pediatric guidance supports optional pacifier use while prioritizing effective feeding and respecting refusal. Advice to wait for established breastfeeding is based on how feeding is going, not a date that guarantees success.

Safe-sleep guidance includes offering a pacifier but advises against coatings, forced acceptance and attachments. Product safety, caregiver support and assessment of illness remain important whether or not the baby uses one.

How BeMama can help

Try one calm offer if you wish, then follow your baby’s response. Keep another comfort option and a plan for getting a short break, so accepting a pacifier never becomes the only way the day can work.

When to seek help

Do not delay feeds, force or secure a pacifier in the mouth, add honey, or attach cords. Pacifier refusal accompanied by feeding difficulty or illness needs assessment; urgent symptoms need urgent care.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • A pacifier is optional comfort, not a feeding substitute or developmental requirement.
  • Choose a calm moment and stop if the baby resists or becomes distressed.
  • Skip coatings, surprise swaps and tugging routines intended to overcome refusal.
  • Use an intact, suitable product and follow safe-sleep guidance.
  • Build other comfort options and seek support when crying or feeding worries you.

Frequently asked questions

Is it a problem if my baby never wants a pacifier?

Not by itself. Babies have different preferences. Continue meeting feeding and comfort needs and use the same safe sleep environment whether or not a pacifier is accepted.

Do I have to wait exactly four weeks?

No single date applies to every baby. For direct breastfeeding, focus on comfortable, effective feeds, adequate supply and appropriate growth. Ask your feeding team if you are unsure.

Should I keep trying when my baby spits it out?

You may offer it another time if you wish, but do not keep pushing through refusal. Turning away, gagging or becoming upset are reasons to stop and try another form of comfort.

Can I dip it in breast milk or formula?

Offer it clean and uncoated. A familiar taste is not necessary, and NICHD safe-sleep guidance advises against coatings. Never use honey or sweeteners to persuade a baby to accept it.

Why is honey on a pacifier unsafe?

Honey can expose babies younger than twelve months to spores that cause infant botulism. A small amount or a honey-containing pacifier is not a safe exception.

Should I switch from the breast before the baby notices?

No. Attend to the feeding need first and offer the pacifier separately if appropriate. A quick swap should not be used to shorten a feed or disguise an offer the baby resists.

Will pulling on it teach my baby to keep it in?

You do not need a tugging routine. Let the baby suck voluntarily, and stop when they release it or resist. Inspecting a product outside the mouth is a separate safety task.

Do I need to put it back throughout the night?

No. Once the baby is asleep, a fallen pacifier does not need to be reinserted. Do not attach cords or toys to keep it within reach.

Can it help me make feeds farther apart?

It should not be used for that purpose. A baby showing hunger cues needs attention to feeding, even if they fed recently. Ask for support if you are worried about intake or feeding patterns.

What if refusing the pacifier is new and feeds are difficult too?

Contact the baby’s clinician. A change affecting sucking, feeding, alertness or growth deserves assessment rather than repeated pacifier attempts. Seek urgent or emergency care for the warning signs described above.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
